title: Under the Same Lantern
subtitle: Jasmine After Rain · Chapter 34 of 40
content:
The lantern seller wanted to charge Iroh twice as much because he recognized him.

I knew the moment it happened. The seller's shoulders went stiff, and his gaze moved from the old man's face to the fine embroidery at his collar.

"For the Dragon of the West," he said, "this one would be appropriate."

He lifted a lantern with enormous painted flames. It was beautiful in the way an expensive decoration could be beautiful when someone else was paying for it. Iroh studied it with grave interest.

"I was considering the little turtleduck," he said.

The seller looked baffled. The turtleduck lantern was crooked, inexpensive, and painted with one eye slightly larger than the other.

I loved it immediately.

"That one," I said.

"Of course," the seller replied, recovering. "For your companion."

The word made me hesitate. It wasn't wrong, but the market was crowded. People knew Iroh; some of them also knew enough about his history to be curious. I had no intention of turning an evening's walk into a public explanation of who loved whom.

Iroh noticed my pause.

"Would you prefer we look elsewhere?" he asked.

"No. I want the turtleduck."

"Then we shall have the turtleduck."

He paid the marked price and accepted change, despite the seller's attempt to refuse it. I carried the lantern while he carried a paper bag of steamed buns. We had promised Mina we would not return to the shop with a pile of unbudgeted decorations, so we were already operating at the very edge of our allowance.

"She will be merciless," I said.

"She has that right."

"She'll say you bought an animal that can't swim."

"It is a lantern. Its swimming abilities are not relevant."

The market curved along the river, where strings of smaller lights reflected in black water. Children ran between stalls. A pair of musicians played an uneven tune near the bridge. A woman selling ribbons called out that she had one shade of gold left before closing.

Iroh offered me his arm.

I wanted it. I also wanted the option to let go if the crowd became too much.

"Yes," I said, slipping my hand around his elbow. "But if someone starts asking personal questions, I get to stop the conversation."

"Agreed."

"And you don't have to introduce me as anything you're uncomfortable saying."

He stopped walking.

"I am not ashamed of you."

"I didn't say you were."

"No." He considered. "You are asking me not to turn my pride into an announcement you did not choose."

"Exactly."

A child nearly collided with my knees while chasing a loose lantern. Iroh caught the lantern by its handle, handed it back, and asked the child to walk near the water. He didn't offer a speech about rivers. The child ran off anyway. We shared a look.

"An excellent success," he said.

"Your authority is terrifying."

We passed a familiar voice. Ren stood at a stall buying stationery, her arms full of papers. She greeted Iroh with a discreet nod, then looked at me.

"Enjoying the festival?"

"I am," I said. "Especially because he hasn't tried to buy the whole street."

"Give him time."

Iroh sighed. "I am surrounded by critics."

Ren left with a smile. She didn't ask about our plans or the relationships I'd spoken about privately with Iroh. Not every person who knew him needed to know everything about us.

A small group had gathered beside the musicians, debating whether to hang a row of lanterns across the narrow market passage. The seller who owned the next stall objected; the string would catch the awning every time he lowered it.

Iroh looked at the empty space above the crowd.

"Perhaps if we tie it higher," he began.

"Then the ladder will block the street," I said.

The seller nodded, grateful someone had noticed.

We walked around the stalls until we found a wider arch where the musicians could still see the display. The lantern maker offered to lend a safer string, but only if somebody agreed to collect it before the market closed. Ren took the evening shift after checking her own plans.

"An evening of extraordinary negotiations," Iroh murmured.

"All so a turtleduck can glow."

He lifted the crooked lantern. "A very noble turtleduck."

The children passing beneath the arch laughed at its uneven eye. One asked whether she could carry it in the procession. Iroh looked at me.

"Does she want to?" I asked her.

"Only to the bridge."

"Then ask the lantern keeper whether it's allowed."

It was. The child carried the lantern a short distance, handed it back carefully, and ran to catch up with her family. We walked behind her, with our hands almost touching.

Iroh glanced at me. "Are you worried about being seen together?"

"Not with you. I'm worried about strangers deciding what being seen means they can ask."

"Then we need not answer."

I smiled. Our relationship had room for public tenderness and private choices. I'd told him openly that I preferred polyamory and was ethically non-monogamous, and he hadn't treated that truth as a riddle for the market to solve.

When the slower music began, he offered his hand again. I took it. There were no speeches, only his ridiculous lantern, a tune we could barely follow, and the faint warmth of his fingers around mine.

Farther along, the musicians started a slower song. Iroh offered his hand. "Would you dance?"

"Here?"

"Unless you have another river in mind."

"I'm terrible."

"Then we will be terrible together."

We danced beside the railing. It was more of a careful shuffle than anything that could be called elegant, and I laughed when he misjudged a step and nearly turned the turtleduck upside down. He caught my hand before I could trip. I caught his sleeve. We steadied each other, still laughing.

For a moment I forgot we were being watched at all. Then I noticed a couple smiling from a nearby bench. I felt the old instinct to explain myself, to describe every other relationship so nobody would assume this was the only person in my life.

I didn't owe them that. Neither did Iroh.

"I like being here with you," I said.

He rested his forehead briefly against mine. "And I with you."

"What if people misunderstand?"

"Then we can correct what matters, and let the rest pass."

"That sounds dangerously reasonable."

"I am occasionally afflicted."

He asked before kissing me. I answered by taking one small step closer. The kiss tasted of sweet bun and cold evening air. A nearby musician missed a note; Iroh laughed against my cheek, and that made me laugh too.

We walked home beneath the lanterns without pretending our public affection had resolved every private agreement. I was still ethically non-monogamous, still happiest with polyamory, and still free to make plans with other people who knew and chose that arrangement. Iroh knew, and he had the same freedom to name his own needs.

The walk back took us through the narrow row of candle stalls. An older vendor was extinguishing his lanterns one by one, careful to save the short wicks for the following night. As we passed, his eyes lingered on Iroh and then on our joined hands.

“General,” he said softly, “my brother served under you.”

I felt Iroh's fingers loosen. He didn't pull away. “I hope your brother came home.”

“He did.” The vendor took down another lantern. “He never spoke about that winter. Not until the day he died.”

I didn't know whether to stand still or keep walking. Iroh's face had become very quiet.

“I am sorry for what he carried,” he said.

The man looked at our turtleduck lantern. Its crooked eye threw a ridiculous shadow across the stones.

“People say you changed,” the vendor continued. “I suppose that's something.”

“It is not a receipt for what happened before.”

The vendor gave one short nod. Neither of them asked me to smooth over the silence. We bought a fresh wick at the ordinary posted price, and the man wrapped it in a scrap of paper without offering further judgment.

Around the corner Iroh stopped. He looked down at our hands.

“Would you prefer I let go when someone recognizes me?” he asked.

“No. But you can tell me when you need a minute.”

He laughed without much humor. “I seem to need several.”

“Then we can take several.”

We stood beneath the awning while a little rain returned. I touched the damp edge of his cuff. He lifted it and kissed my fingers once, with none of the polished amusement he'd used at the lantern stall. I loved that the gesture was awkward. It meant he hadn't prepared it for an audience.

When we moved again, he held my hand as lightly as before. We carried the wick and the crooked turtleduck home instead of trying to carry the vendor's whole history.


At the shop, Mina saw the turtleduck and put both hands on her hips.

"How much?"

"The price on the tag," I said.

Iroh looked proud of himself.

"Good," Mina said. "Then tomorrow you can help me fix its crooked eye."

We hung it above the long table, where it cast a small, uneven pool of light. Later he invited me upstairs. I said yes, and we left the door closed on the part of the evening that didn't belong to the market.

By morning the turtleduck had become Mina's favorite lantern. She would never admit it, but she moved it away from the stove so the heat couldn't scorch the paint. I saw Iroh notice. Neither of us said a word.
